name: Bemotrizinol

lead: Bemotrizinol is an oil-soluble sunscreen filter that covers both UVB and UVA and is very photostable, so protection holds through the day. Skincare enthusiasts seek it out in EU, Australian and Asian products to limit photoaging and pigmentation.

It absorbs UV across about 280-400 nm, converts it to heat and helps stabilise filters like avobenzone. It has been approved in the EU since 2000. Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement of approval for US sunscreens on 9 June 2026.

paras: It is used in daily sunscreens, often imported or chosen from non-US brands, and blended with other filters.
Registered trials of a 6% sunscreen examined absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. Lab studies found no estrogenic activity, and aquatic toxicity studies exist.

angle.text: Bemotrizinol is a photostable UVA and UVB filter, so the sunscreen keeps working through the day and less photoaging and pigmentation builds up. Support comes from sunscreen testing and long regional use.

lead: Bemotrizinol (INCI: bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, BEMT; trade names Tinosorb S, Escalol S, Parsol Shield) is an oil-soluble organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA, with absorption peaks around 310 and 340-345 nm.[1][2] It is noted for photostability and for helping stabilise less stable filters such as avobenzone.[2]

It has been approved in the European Union since 2000 and in Australia, and is widely used in sunscreens there and in parts of Asia.[1][2] For years it was absent from US sunscreens because it was not in the FDA's monograph; Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement of approval for sunscreens on 9 June 2026.[2]

Human data include a series of 2020-2022 trials registered for a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen, covering absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. No trial has studied it for appearance outcomes beyond sun protection.

paras: Bemotrizinol is used in sunscreens and daily moisturisers with SPF. A water-phase version, Tinosorb S Aqua, embeds the compound in a PMMA matrix dispersed in water so it can be added to the water phase of a formulation.[2]

An in vitro ranking of EU-authorised filters at their maximum permitted concentrations placed bemotrizinol as the most effective by SPF contribution, according to Wikipedia's citation of a 2007 study.[2] About 98.4% remains intact after 50 minimal erythemal doses of UV, and it shows SPF synergy with bisoctrizole, ethylhexyl triazone and iscotrizinol.[2]

In vitro studies have examined it in nanostructured lipid carriers and nanoemulsions for penetration and photostability,[3] in sprayable emulsions at high filter concentrations,[4] and in combination with retinyl palmitate for phototoxic risk.[5]

A Phase 3 maximum-usage pharmacokinetic trial of a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen enrolled 162 participants,[6] preceded by a 14-person Phase 1 absorption study.[7] Separate registered trials assessed photoallergy (n=50),[8] phototoxicity (n=34)[9] and irritation, sensitisation and cumulative irritation (n=224).[10] The registry entries themselves do not report outcomes.
Wikipedia states that in vitro and rat uterotrophic assays found no estrogenic activity, unlike some other organic filters.[2]

Bemotrizinol was one of ten filters tested on brine shrimp and marine microalgae in a 2020 study,[11] and triazine UV filters have been identified as pollutants in indoor dust and air in South China.[12]

The EU has permitted it since 2000, and Australia lists it as approved.[2] Wikipedia reports a 9 June 2026 FDA press release announcing its approval for use in sunscreens, whereas Grokipedia, written earlier, described US approval as anticipated.[2][1]

Registered human studies of a 6% bemotrizinol sunscreen cover pharmacokinetics,[6][7] phototoxicity,[9] photoallergy[8] and irritation/sensitisation.[10] A melasma photoprotection trial and a European photopatch study of sunscreen allergens are also registered, though they concern sunscreens broadly.[13][14] No study has tested bemotrizinol as a treatment for appearance concerns.

timeline.event: Approved for use in the European Union.[2]
Phase 1-3 absorption and safety trials registered for a 6% formulation.[7][6]
